title: Building your own software factory — Eric Zakariasson, Cursor
talk_summary: Eric Zakariasson (Cursor) describes building an agent 'software factory': primitives (modular code, in-distribution patterns), guardrails (hooks, dynamically-emerging rules, tests), enablers (skills/MCPs, self-starting dev envs), and isolated per-agent VMs for parallelism. He also shows flywheel automations that mine transcripts and human PR comments to generate rules, and an agentic code-owner that risk-scores PRs to unblock low-risk merges.

takeaways.what_they_do: An agent inspects each PR, classifies risk (rename vs. business-logic change), auto-approves low-risk PRs, and for high-risk pulls in prior authors' feedback instead of blocking on a human code owner.
takeaways.numbers: code owners were right ~80% of the time; the 20% caused bottlenecks

takeaways.what_they_do: A scheduled automation reads past agent transcripts, extracts corrections and preferences, and writes them back as persistent rules so the same correction isn't repeated.
takeaways.evidence_quote: this continual learning plug-in that looks looks through uh the transcripts and store this as a rule

takeaways.technique: Mine human PR comments as high-signal training data
takeaways.what_they_do: An automation reads comments humans leave on merged PRs and stores them so agents learn what reviewers actually care about.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if a human actually goes in and reviews a PR and leaves a comment, there's probably like high high value and high signal

takeaways.technique: Isolated per-agent VMs over shared worktrees
takeaways.what_they_do: Each agent gets its own VM running its own DB/cache/services so parallel changes are pure and side-effect-free, enabling scaling to thousands of agents/day.
takeaways.evidence_quote: just using cloud agents uh where I spawn a VM and this VM can run a database ... to be much better
takeaways.numbers: claims multiple thousands of agents/day at Cursor

takeaways.technique: Agent self-verification via Playwright + computer-use video
takeaways.what_they_do: Agents write and run Playwright e2e tests, and for UI changes drive a browser and return a recording/screenshots so a human can verify outcome without reading code.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the agent created this uh end to end tests um using a playright so it can just spawn browsers

takeaways.technique: Frontload context via specs; plan sync, execute async
takeaways.what_they_do: Managers write long specs/plans up front, then dispatch agents asynchronously, keeping 5-10 running while doing synchronous planning.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you kind of like frontload uh the context to the agents either through like a plan or a long spec
takeaways.numbers: 5-10 agents running in parallel per engineer
